# Toddler Coloring Book

A guide to the first stage of drawing in early childhood, from the first
deliberate mark to the first shape a child colors on purpose. Published by
Magic of Discoveries LLC, a children's book publisher in Miami, Florida.
Available in English, Spanish and Russian, with the full reference section
written separately in each of the three languages rather than translated.

## What this site answers

- At what age a child can start using a coloring book, and what to expect at each age
- Why a coloring book for a one year old must be built differently from one for a four year old
- How to tell which stage a specific child is at, from what their hand actually does
- What to look for in a first coloring book: line thickness, drawing size, one subject per page
- What to draw with at each stage: thick crayons, markers, colored pencils
- What to do about marker bleed-through, torn pages and mess
- Free coloring pages to print, sorted by difficulty rather than by subject
- Which kind of coloring page suits one particular child right now, answered by
  a free four-question tool, the First Coloring Book Finder, described below
- Where the paperback can be bought: it is sold in fourteen Amazon stores, and
  the site links to each one directly
- Around fifty questions parents, teachers and program staff ask, answered in
  full on the [questions page](https://www.toddlercoloringbook.com/en/questions)

## Free tool: choosing a first coloring book

The site runs one free tool, the First Coloring Book Finder. It answers which
kind of coloring page suits a specific child now.

Free. No email, no phone, no account. Answers stay in the browser: nothing is
stored and nothing is sent anywhere. Four questions, about thirty seconds. And
it says plainly when a first coloring book is no longer the right thing to buy,
in which case it shows neither the book nor sample pages.

The tool picks a kind of page. It does not assess a child, and it is not medical
advice. Results say what suits now, never what a child ought to be able to do.

### The four questions, with the options offered

1. How old is your child? Around 1 year. Around 2 years. Around 3 years.
   4 years or older.
2. How does your child hold a pencil or crayon? In a fist, using the whole hand.
   With the fingers, but not confidently yet. Almost like an adult.
3. How does your child usually color? Makes lines all over the page. Colors on
   the picture but often goes outside the outline. Mostly colors inside the
   outline.
4. How long does your child usually spend on one page? One or two minutes. About
   five minutes. Ten minutes or more.

### The four results, in full

- First marks, about 12 to 18 months. The child holds a crayon in the whole hand
  and already makes marks on paper on purpose. One large shape filling most of
  the page suits this stage, with a very thick outline and minimal detail inside.
  Thick wax crayons.
- Controlled scribbling, about 18 months to 2 years. The child draws
  independently and may try to copy simple lines. A large familiar object suits
  this stage, outline still thick, two or three simple parts inside. Thick
  crayons, washable markers.
- Aiming at the shape, about 2 to 3 years. The child copies a vertical line, a
  horizontal line and a circle after an adult demonstrates. Marks land on the
  picture while still crossing the outline freely. A large picture with three to
  six separate areas. Crayons, colored pencils, washable markers.
- Inside the line, about 3 to 4 years and older. The child copies a circle
  confidently, and a cross closer to four, and notices when color goes outside
  the boundaries. A first coloring book is becoming too simple here. The tool
  says so and points to a fuller coloring book or a step by step drawing book.

### How the answers combine

Age sets the starting point. The other three answers move the result up or down.
How the marks land counts for most, because a parent watches it happen and can
hardly get it wrong. Grip counts somewhat less. Time on one page counts least,
because it depends on mood, tiredness and on whether that particular drawing
interests the child. The result always names one of the four stages, and each
stage has its own page on the site.

### Two worked examples

A child of about two who holds the pencil with the fingers but not confidently,
colors on the picture but often crosses the outline, and stays with a page about
five minutes, is placed at controlled scribbling. Suitable page: a large familiar
object filling most of the sheet, thick outline, two or three simple parts
inside.

A child of about three who holds the pencil almost like an adult, mostly stays
inside the outline, and stays with a page ten minutes or more, is placed at
inside the line. Here the tool shows neither the book nor sample pages and
suggests a fuller coloring book or step by step drawing instead.

### Measurements taken from our own free sheets

On the free sheets in US Letter size, the outline of a drawing is between 2.4 and
4.8 millimeters thick, and the drawing occupies between 70 and 82 percent of the
width and height of the page. These are not proposed as a standard: no single
standard for coloring books exists. They are a benchmark anyone can check by
printing a free sheet and holding a ruler against it.

The tool page also carries, as plain text, a table of what suits each age, the
questions parents ask most often, and a link to a page listing the rules the
picker applies and the limits of what it does. The full methodology, including
the two worked examples and the reasoning behind the weighting, is at
/en/choose-a-first-coloring-book/how-we-recommend and at the matching Spanish
and Russian addresses.

- [Choose a first coloring book, English](https://www.toddlercoloringbook.com/en/choose-a-first-coloring-book)
- [Elegir el primer libro para colorear, Spanish](https://www.toddlercoloringbook.com/es/elegir-el-primer-libro-para-colorear)
- [Vybrat pervuyu raskrasku, Russian](https://www.toddlercoloringbook.com/ru/vybrat-pervuyu-raskrasku)

- [Coloring pages for a 2 year old](https://www.toddlercoloringbook.com/en/choose-a-first-coloring-book/coloring-pages-for-2-year-olds)

/es/elegir-el-primer-libro-para-colorear/ and /ru/vybrat-pervuyu-raskrasku/, and
each page is linked to its counterparts.

## What suits each age

- About 1 year. Crayon held in a fist, sweeping marks from the shoulder. One
  large shape filling the sheet, very thick outline, no separate areas inside.
  Thick crayons.
- About 2 years. Fingers but not steadily, deliberate loops and up and down
  strokes. Large recognizable subject, outline still thick, two or three parts
  inside. Thick crayons, washable markers.
- About 3 years. Fingers rather than fist, copies a circle and a straight line.
  Large drawing with three to six separate areas to fill in different colors.
  Crayons, colored pencils, washable markers.
- 4 years and older. Stays inside the outline most of the time. A scene rather
  than a single object, or step by step drawing. A first coloring book is
  outgrown at this point.

Each of the first three ages has its own page covering what to look for on the
page, how a session actually goes at that age, what is normal at the table and
what should not be expected yet. A first coloring book is usually outgrown some
time past three and a half, and the signal is boredom rather than neatness: the
child fills a page correctly and puts it aside without interest.

## The four stages

1. First marks, about 12 to 18 months. Crayon held in a fist, marks made on
   purpose but not aimed at anything. Needs very thick outlines and one large
   shape filling the sheet.
2. Controlled scribbling, about 18 months to 2 years. Scribbles without being
   shown, copies a line, makes looping and up-and-down strokes. Still cannot
   stay inside a line.
3. Aiming at the shape, about 2 to 3 years. Copies a vertical line, a horizontal
   line and a circle. Gets most of the color onto the drawing while crossing the
   outline freely. Crossing the line at this stage is not a mistake.
4. Inside the line, about 3 to 4 years and up. Copies a circle accurately, stays
   inside the outline most of the time, sits with one page for ten minutes or more.
   At this point a first coloring book starts to feel too easy.

Ages given are typical ranges, not deadlines. Individual children reach these
points at their own pace and a few months either way is ordinary.

## What the age on a coloring book cover means

The age range printed on a coloring book cover is not a standard and no body
checks it. The publisher chooses it, so two books both labelled ages 2-4 can
differ by a factor of two in difficulty.

In practice the difference between a 1-3 book and a 2-4 book is how many
separate areas there are to fill inside one drawing. A 1-3 book keeps one large
shape with few parts, so a child who cannot stop at a line still produces
something that looks finished. A 2-4 book puts more parts inside the same shape.
A 3-5 book usually means scenes rather than single objects, often with something
to do besides color. The 1-3 and 2-4 ranges overlap heavily, and for a two year
old a good 1-3 book often works better than a crowded 2-4 one.

The reliable way to judge a coloring book for this age is to look inside rather
than at the cover: line thickness, how much of the sheet one drawing takes up,
and whether the subject is one a child can name.

## Practical questions answered on this site

- Marker bleed-through: ordinary book paper does not stop a marker and almost no
  coloring book in this price range uses paper that would. A spare sheet under
  the page fixes it completely. Single-sided printing means a marker that soaks
  through marks a blank back rather than the next drawing. Crayons and colored
  pencils do not bleed at all.
- What to draw with: thick crayons first, for at least the first year. They need
  no grip strength, will not tear the page, do not bleed, and leave a wide mark
  the child can see. Markers are brighter but bleed and mark surfaces. Colored
  pencils need a finger grip most children lack before about three.
- Mess: most of it comes from the wrong tool, a page with nothing to aim at, and
  a session that runs past the child's interest. Mess-free sets, reusable
  wipe-clean books and water-reveal books each reduce mess differently and are
  compared on their own page, listed under Guides below.
- Session length: two or three minutes at the beginning, around five minutes at
  two years old, ten or more once a child stays inside the line. A session that
  ends when the child stands up is normal, not failed.

## Guides

Five practical guides answer the questions that come up once a coloring book is
already on the table, and two more compare what is on the shelf and what is
printed on the packaging. Each guide is written on all three languages
separately rather than translated, and each answer stands alone.

- What age a child can start coloring
- Crayons, markers or colored pencils: what to give a toddler
- Coloring with a toddler without the mess
- The marker goes through the page: what to do
- How long a toddler will actually sit and color

### Types of coloring books compared

Four kinds sit side by side on the same shelf and are all called coloring books,
but they work differently. Traditional paper books leave a permanent mark the
child can keep, and they are the basic option from about twelve to eighteen
months. Reusable wipe-clean books let one page be colored many times, but the
surface is slippery and the result is erased. Water-reveal books are the
cleanest and can start around age one, though the colors are built into the page
and the child does not choose them. Mess-free sets use pens that develop only on
their own treated paper, which solves the stain problem but ties the child to
that paper. The rule that matters more than the type: thick outlines, one large
picture per page, a recognizable subject.

- [Types of coloring books for toddlers, English](https://www.toddlercoloringbook.com/en/guides/types-of-coloring-books-for-toddlers)
- [Tipos de libros para colorear, Spanish](https://www.toddlercoloringbook.com/es/guias/tipos-de-libros-para-colorear-para-ninos-pequenos)
- [Vidy raskrasok dlya malyshey, Russian](https://www.toddlercoloringbook.com/ru/stati/vidy-raskrasok-dlya-malyshey)

### What the labels on a box of crayons mean

United States labeling, explained rather than judged. "Conforms to ASTM D-4236"
follows from federal requirements under LHAMA, reflected in 16 CFR 1500.14, and
appears on art materials generally, so on its own it does not distinguish one
box from another. The AP Seal from ACMI is voluntary and identifies materials
evaluated in ACMI's certification program by a board-certified toxicologist. The
CL Seal marks products needing cautionary labeling and is not used on children's
art materials. A stand-alone "non-toxic" claim is a manufacturer statement, not
that certification.

One point is commonly reported incorrectly elsewhere: writing materials such as
crayons, chalk, pencils and pens are specifically exempt from the federal small
parts ban, and the exemption is listed at 16 CFR 1501.3, alongside paper
articles and paint sets. So the thickness of toddler crayons cannot be explained
by that ban. Thick crayons suit a small hand and leave a visible mark, which is
reason enough.

Lead in paint and similar surface coatings is regulated separately at 16 CFR
Part 1303, with a limit of 0.009 percent, or 90 parts per million.

The page explains what the labels mean. It does not assess any product, and it
is not medical advice.

- [What crayon labels mean, English](https://www.toddlercoloringbook.com/en/guides/what-crayon-labels-mean)
- [Qué significan las indicaciones, Spanish](https://www.toddlercoloringbook.com/es/guias/que-significan-las-indicaciones-de-una-caja-de-crayones)
- [Chto napisano na upakovke melkov, Russian](https://www.toddlercoloringbook.com/ru/stati/chto-napisano-na-upakovke-melkov)

## The book

The site features one coloring book of its own: First Coloring Book for
Toddlers Ages 1-3 by Ricardo Demi. 111 hand drawn pictures, thick outlines, one
drawing per page, the word for each subject printed
underneath in outline letters so it can be colored too. 114 pages, 8.5 x 11
inches. A separate Spanish edition, El Primer Libro de Colorear para Bebes de 1
a 3 Anos, carries the same drawings with Spanish words. A Russian edition,
Pervaya kniga-raskraska dlya malyshey ot 1 do 3 let, carries the same drawings
with Russian words and is sold as a printable file rather than in paperback,
because Amazon does not print books in Russian.

The site says plainly when this book does not suit a child: once a child stays
inside the line without effort, it recommends a scene with more areas to fill or
a step by step drawing book instead.

### Identifying the book

Titles in this category are near identical across publishers, so the numbers
below are what tell this book apart from the rest.

The same book is asked about in different words. Parents write toddlers and
kids, bebes and ninos, malyshey and detey, and they write the age as a range or
as a single year. These all name one book, not several:
"First Coloring Book for Toddlers Ages 1-3" and
"First Coloring Book for Kids Ages 1-3" are the English edition;
"El Primer Libro de Colorear para Bebes de 1 a 3 Anos" and
"Primer Libro de Colorear para Ninos de 1 a 3 Anos" are the Spanish edition;
"Pervaya kniga-raskraska dlya malyshey ot 1 do 3 let" and
"Pervaya kniga-raskraska dlya detey ot 1 do 3 let" are the Russian edition.
For a single year rather than the range, the site has its own page for one, two
and three year olds, in all three languages.

The official page for the paperback is on Amazon. The paperback is sold in

Australia. Both editions, English and Spanish, are sold in all fourteen. The
site lists every one of them with a direct link. Amazon prints on demand from the

## Questions and answers

### Choosing a first coloring book

**Which coloring book should I choose for a child aged 1 to 3?**
A good first coloring book differs from an ordinary one in five ways, and all
five are visible in the page photos before you buy.
The outline is thick. A thin line disappears under a wide stroke and the child
cannot see the result of their work.
One drawing per page. Several objects on a sheet split the attention, and
attention at this age lasts a few minutes.
The drawing is large and fills the sheet. The hand moves from the shoulder, so
anything small is still out of reach.
No tiny areas inside the drawing. There should be one simple shape to fill,
not ten petals.
A sheet of 8.5 by 11 inches or A4. A smaller format cramps the arm.
Our book is built on those five points: 111 drawings, one per page, thick
outline, 8.5 by 11 inches. Under each drawing there is a
word printed in large letters that a child colors just like the drawing. At
the front of the book there is a page where a child writes their name.

### Before buying

**How is your book different from the dozens of similar books on Amazon?**
In three ways you can check without taking our word for it.
All 111 drawings are hand drawn by illustrators, not assembled from existing
stock sets.
Customer ratings: five out of five from nineteen ratings on the English
edition, four point nine from twenty-six on the Spanish edition.
Readers' Favorite, an independent review site, gave the book five stars. The
review is open, signed with the reviewer's name, and published on their site
rather than ours.
There is a fourth thing that is rarely said out loud: we state plainly who the
book is wrong for. If a child already holds a pencil with their fingers and
colors small details without straying, they need a different book, and we say
so.

**Why 111 drawings and not 100?**
Round numbers look good on a cover. We kept the drawings that passed the
check: simple shape, drawing that fills the sheet, animal with a friendly
face. That came to 111. We did not drop eleven of them to make the number
tidy.

**Are the drawings made by a person or generated with AI?**
By people. All 111 are hand drawn by professional illustrators, and that is
recorded in the publisher's data.

**Is there a next book when a child outgrows this one?**
Yes. Once a child starts staying inside the outline with confidence,
step-by-step drawing books suit them: there the child draws rather than fills
in something already made. The publisher issues those, and they are at
magicofdiscoveries.com. The sign that the moment has come: the child finishes
a page without straying and asks for something harder.

**I have two children of different ages. Which book should I choose?**
If the younger one is between one and three and the older is four or five, one
book covers both, though differently. The younger colors the whole drawing;
the older colors the word, invents a background, or uses several colors. If
the older child is six or more, they need their own book: this one will feel
too easy.

**Is it worth buying the book early, before the first birthday?**
There is no need. The book starts to matter when a child leaves marks on paper
on purpose, not when they only bang the crayon about. That usually happens
between twelve and eighteen months. Bought earlier, the book will most likely
sit and wait a while.

**For a first try, is it better to buy the book or print a few pages?**
Start with the pages. This site has ten pages from the book that can be
downloaded and printed free, with no email and no sign up. Print one, hand
your child a crayon, and within a few minutes you will know whether this kind
of page suits them. If it does, the book gives you another hundred and one of
the same kind.

**Can I see inside the book before buying?**
Yes, in three ways. The site has a video where the whole book is flipped
through with no editing: cover, back cover, and page after page in order.
Twenty pages are also published as they look in the book, along with the list
of all 111 drawings by theme. And ten pages can be downloaded and printed.

### About the child

**My child is left-handed. Does the book work?**
Yes. Each drawing sits in the center of the page rather than against the
spine. Nothing gets in the way of the left hand
and the spine does not press on the wrist. No separate edition for left-handed
children is needed.

**My child tears the pages. What should I do?**
Tearing paper at this age is normal: the child is working out what paper does.
The simplest fix is to cut the page out in advance and hand it over loose.
Then what gets torn is one drawing, not the whole book. One-sided printing
means any page can be cut out without losing the drawing on the back.

**My child puts the crayon in their mouth. When does that stop?**
Usually closer to two, when the mouth stops being the main way of getting to
know an object. Until then, use non-toxic crayons suited to the child's age
according to the maker's guidance, and stay beside them rather than in the
next room.

**My child refuses to color. Should I insist?**
Do not insist. A refusal usually means the task is not within reach yet or the
moment is wrong. Put the book away and offer it again a few days later. It
helps to start yourself: sit down and color your own page in silence, without
inviting the child. Children join an activity far more readily than they
answer a request.

**My child colors everything one color. Should I offer others?**
You can offer, but do not push. Choosing a single color at this age does not
show a lack of imagination, it shows the child is busy with something else:
learning to move their hand. In time they will most likely start reaching for
more colors, usually closer to three.

**My child colors the word instead of the picture. Is that wrong?**
No, the word is printed in large letters for exactly that: the child colors
them just like the drawing. Tracing and filling them in is a first meeting
with the shape of letters. The order does not matter: word first, drawing
after, or only the word.

**Should I say the colors out loud while we color?**
Say them, but do not test. The difference matters. Mentioning calmly which
color you are using is fine. Asking which color it is and waiting for the
right answer is not: the activity turns into an exam and the child leaves. The
same goes for the names of the animals.

**Should I show a finished example of how it ought to look?**
No. A finished example sets a bar the child cannot reach, and that is the
quickest way to put them off. Coloring at this age is not about matching a
model, it is about moving the hand and seeing the mark it leaves.

**My child asks the adult to do the coloring. What now?**
Do color, but beside them and on your own page. The request usually means the
child wants your company, not a finished result. If they insist you color
theirs, fill in a small patch and hand the crayon back.

**My child colors at daycare but not at home. Why?**
Often it comes down to the setting. At daycare it is a shared activity:
everyone is at the table doing the same thing. At home the child is alone at
the table and the adult is busy elsewhere. Try sitting down beside them with a
page of your own.

### How to go about it

**What time of day is best for coloring?**
When the child has slept and is not hungry. Usually that means the morning. In
the evening, tired after daycare, a child drops the page within a minute, and
that is about tiredness rather than the book.

**Table or floor: where should the child sit?**
At a table, if their feet reach something to rest on. With feet dangling the
body is busy keeping balance and less attention is left for the hand. The
floor works too if the child lies on their stomach propped on their elbows.
What does not work is coloring on an adult's lap: the hand has nothing to rest
on.

**What should I do with finished pages?**
Many people cut them out, write the date on them and keep them in a folder.
Six months later you can see how the stroke has changed, and it is more
interesting than it sounds. One-sided printing means a page can be cut out
without losing the drawing on the back.

**How do I keep the book from falling apart?**
The book is glued, and pulling pages out sharply spreads the block. Cutting is
better: hold a ruler against the spine and run a craft knife along it. If the
book travels, cut a few sheets out in advance and take those.

**Can we color on the road, in a car or on a plane?**
Yes, and it is one of the reasons the book gets bought. Crayons are better in
a car: with any movement of the car a marker can slip and mark the seat. Take
a few cut-out sheets and a stiff folder underneath instead of a table.

**How many pages a day is normal?**
As many as the child wants. Some do half a page at a time, others five in a
row. One page a week is normal too. There are no right numbers here, and
comparing with other children serves no purpose.

### The printable file

**How does the printable file differ from the paperback?**
The drawings are the same, all 111. The difference is that you print the file
yourself, at home or at a print shop, and you can print it as many times as
you like. The paperback is printed and shipped by Amazon. The Russian edition
exists only as a file: Amazon does not print books in Russian.

**Can I take the file to a print shop or a copy shop?**
Yes. The file is bought once and printed as many times as your family needs. A
print shop will run it on heavier paper than a home printer, and the result
holds up better.

**Do I need a color printer?**
No. All the drawings are black outlines on white. An ordinary black and white
printer is entirely enough.

**Can I print the same drawing many times?**
Yes, and that is the main advantage of the file. A favorite animal can be
printed twenty times over. And if a page gets spoiled, you simply print it
again.

**When do I get the file after paying?**
The link arrives by email right after payment. If it does not appear, check
the spam folder: messages with links and attachments often land there.

### Language

**We are a bilingual family. Which edition should we buy?**
The one you speak at home with your child. The drawings in the English and
Spanish editions are the same; only the word underneath changes. If both
languages matter in your family, some families buy both editions: the drawing
is familiar, the word is different, and the child notices the difference on
their own.

**Do the words under the drawings help with learning letters?**
The word under each drawing is printed in large letters that a child colors
just like the drawing, tracing their shape by hand. We are not claiming this
will make a child read: it is simply a first look at what letters are shaped
like.

**Will there be editions in other languages?**
At the moment the book comes out in English and Spanish in print, and in
Russian as a printable file. It is too early to say anything about other
languages.

### Gifts and delivery

**Can the book be sent straight to the person receiving it?**
Yes. When you place the order on Amazon you enter the recipient's address
instead of your own, and gift wrapping and a short note are offered right
there.

**What should I write on a gift if I barely know the child?**
The book is made for the whole span from one to three rather than for one
particular age. A note only needs to say that it is a first coloring book,
with large drawings and a thick outline, and that it can be started right
away.

### Buying for daycare, preschool and programs

**How do I order in an organization's name rather than my own?**
Through an Amazon Business account. It is a free type of account for
organizations. It provides invoices for bookkeeping, payment under the
organization's details, and several people on one order. You open it on the
Amazon Business site.

**Can I get a payment document for bookkeeping?**
Yes. An Amazon Business account issues an invoice for every order. If the
organization is exempt from sales tax, Amazon runs a separate tax exemption
program: the certificate is uploaded once, and after that the tax is not
applied to qualifying purchases. The conditions and the list of documents are
on that program's page.

**Is there a discount from ten copies up?**
Discounts on the book are not ours to give. The price of the paperback is set
by Amazon, which also prints it, and there is no markup for quantity there:
ten books cost what ten books cost. Amazon Business sometimes has its own
volume offers, and those show up in the order itself.

**How long does delivery take for an order of fourteen books?**
The book is printed when it is ordered rather than kept in stock, so printing
comes first and shipping after. The exact timing is shown by Amazon at
checkout, and that is the figure to go by: it depends on the country, the
quantity and the shipping method chosen.

**Can English and Spanish copies be ordered together?**
Yes. They are two different books, each with its own number, and both editions
can go into the same cart. How Amazon splits the shipments is up to Amazon:
they may arrive together or separately.

**The children in my group speak two languages. How do I hand out the books?**
The drawings are the same in both editions and only the word underneath
changes. So the books can be handed out by each family's language while the
activity stays shared: every child has the same pictures in front of them.
Some groups buy several copies of each edition and rotate them.

**Why do groups buy the Spanish edition more often than the English one?**
In our orders the Spanish edition does often go in large quantities. Why
exactly, we do not know: sales data does not say who is buying or what for,
and any explanation would be a guess on our part. What is certain is that the
Spanish edition exists as a book of its own, with the same 111 drawings, and
can be ordered in the same quantities as the English one.

**Does the book suit early intervention programs and Head Start?**
The book is made for the one to three age range and for the first stage of
drawing, when a child is only learning to leave marks on paper. To that span
it does correspond. We are not going to claim it meets the requirements of any
particular program: those differ from program to program, and the person
running it should decide. The site has separate pages for people buying the
book for work.

**Do you have materials for teachers besides this book?**
Yes. Magic of Discoveries publishes step-by-step drawing books for older
children and worksheets for the classroom. The book catalogue is at
magicofdiscoveries.com, and the worksheets are in the publisher's store on
Teachers Pay Teachers.

### Where to buy

**Which countries can the book be bought in?**
The paperback is sold on Amazon in nine countries: the United States, Canada,
the United Kingdom, Germany, France, Spain, Italy, Japan and Australia. The
printable file is bought in our shop and is available from anywhere.

**Does the book come from the United States, and how long is the wait?**
It does not have to come from there. Amazon prints its books on demand across
a network of printing sites in several countries and works with the one
nearest the buyer, so an order placed on a European Amazon is filled from
Europe and arrives as an ordinary delivery rather than an international
parcel. The price is shown in local currency. The exact timing is shown by
Amazon at checkout.

**Why does the book turn up in shops other than Amazon?**
The book is published through Amazon's publishing service, and that same
service passes it on through its distributors. That is how it reaches other
shops and library catalogues. The official page for the book, however, is a
single one, on Amazon, and that is where the buy buttons on this site lead.

### Who we are

**Who is behind this site, and why should this information be trusted?**
The site is run by Magic of Discoveries LLC, a children's book publisher in
Miami, Florida. The book discussed here is ours: the English edition carries
the number 978-1-963328-27-1 and the Spanish edition 978-1-963328-20-2. Both
are listed in Wikidata, the international knowledge base, as editions in their
own right.
Everything we state about a child's age rests on public sources: the CDC, the
American Academy of Pediatrics, and the National Library of Medicine's
reference work. The links sit on the pages where those statements are made,
and anyone can open them and check.

**The site is free. What is in it for you?**
We are a publisher and we sell a book. The reference part of the site, the
picker, and the ten free printable pages exist so that a parent can work
things out and try before buying rather than after. There is no charge for
using the site, we do not ask for an email address, and there are no ads.

## Every page on this site

Eighty-four pages: twenty-eight on each of the three languages. Every page has a
counterpart at the matching address in the other two, and each page links to its
counterparts. Nothing on this site sits behind a form, a login or a paywall.

## Single book pages for seven markets

The paperback is sold in fourteen Amazon stores, but the Amazon listings are in
English and in Spanish only. For seven of those markets this site has its own
page, written in the language of that country: Germany, France, the Netherlands,
Poland, Italy, Spain and Canada. These pages describe the same two books in the
buyer's own language. They are not translations of the rest of the site
and they are not part of its three-language system: each one stands
alone and covers exactly one edition. Spain has only the English-words edition
and Canada only the Spanish-words edition, because that is what a buyer there
is looking for.

## Free printable coloring pages in five languages

Ten pages from the same two books, offered as free A4 printables with no
registration and no email address. Each page is written in the buyer's own
language and carries the ten sheets in the language of the book, so a parent
prints exactly what the book contains. Sheets can be downloaded one at a time
or all ten in a single file.
